newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-PacDun settles few implant cases.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-PacDun settles few implant cases.

text.p: Industrial group Pacific Dunlop Ltd said on Thursday it had reached financial settlements with some Australians fitted with heart implants made by a U.S. subsidiary.

Pacific Dunlop senior legal counsel Martin Hudson, confirming a local newspaper report of the settlements, said the group's Accufix Research Institute Inc (ARI) had made small payments to a "handful" of Australians fitted with the device.
"They are small in number and they are small in cash amount and they are fully insured," he told Reuters in an interview.
The pacemaker implants, made between 1988 and 1994, are at the centre of a possible major class action in the United States.
A class action is pending in Canada and individual claims on ARI have been made in Australia and elsewhere.
A wire in the pacemaker has been found to have fractured in some patients, leading to six known deaths.
A total of about 23,000 people in the United States received the implants over seven years.
Hudson said the Australian settlements did not imply ARI had accepted any liability in relation to the so-called "J-wires".
"We don't believe we are liable in a strict legal sense," he said.
A recent U.S. court decision has revived a class action against it in the United States, but Hudson said ARI had asked the decision be referred to an appeal court.
About 440 suits involving 600 individuals have been served on ARI in the United States. If these were rolled into a class action, ARI's potential exposure would be much greater.
"While a class is up and running, the U.S. people (plaintiffs) are acting for all, at least living people, who had leads put in," Hudson said.
"That is some number less than 23,000 ..."
So far the parent, Pacific Dunlop, has made no mention of a contingent liability in its own books, saying the subsidiary, ARI, faces all the risk from the legal actions.
ARI is cashed up after last year's A$170 million sale of Telectronics Pacing Systems, the Pacific Dunlop subsidiary which ran the implant business in the United States.
"It (ARI) has the lion's share of that figure," Hudson said, adding that ARI also had "certain insurance proceeds".
"If a subsidiary is sued and successfully, the plaintiff can only recover against the subsidiary. He has no right to recover against the parent company."
ARI wants to deal with each legal claim individually.
"In our view the vast majority of these people have no legal basis on which to sue us, but each matter has to be taken on its merits," Hudson said.

The majority of suits against ARI in the United States cannot be heard before September due to procedural requirements, he said. Hearings in the Canadian class actions are not expected to be heard before next year, he added.
-- Melbourne bureau 613-9286-1421
